Eloquence

EL-uh-kwuhns -- from Latin eloquentia, from eloqui, 'to speak out' (ex- 'out' + loqui 'to speak'). · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Eloquence is fluent, persuasive speaking or writing.

Despite years of stage fright, she discovered a surprising eloquence once she started talking about the cause she loved most.

Worked Example

A nervous best man who has never given a toast before suddenly finds the right words, and the whole room falls silent to listen.

That sudden gift for fluent, persuasive speech is eloquence -- notice that it can appear even in someone with no formal training, once they truly care about what they're saying.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fluency: the ability to speak or write smoothly and easily

oratory: the formal art and skill of public speaking

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

stammering: halting, stumbling speech

incoherence: a lack of clear or logical connection in speech

Where it sits · how persuasive and polished the language is — fluency → eloquence → oratory

fluency vs. eloquence: Fluency simply means being able to speak or write smoothly, without necessarily persuading or moving anyone -- eloquence adds real persuasive polish and grace on top of that basic smoothness.

oratory vs. eloquence: Oratory is stronger and more formal than eloquence -- it specifically names the practiced art of skilled public speaking, while eloquence can appear in an unpolished, everyday moment too.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — e-

Prefix — e-: out (a form of Latin ex-)

Root — loqu

Root — loqu: to speak (from Latin loqui -- the same root in loquacious and colloquial)

Suffix — -ence

Suffix — -ence: the quality or state of (Latin -entia)

Put it together

Put it together: E- ('out') + loqu ('to speak', from Latin loqui) + -ence ('the quality of') spell eloquence: literally the quality of 'speaking out' fully and fluently, letting one's thoughts flow into clear, persuasive words.

Use the root in a new word: loquacious

Use the root in a new word: loquacious: Once the topic turned to baseball, my usually quiet uncle became surprisingly loquacious.

Root Check

Word Choice

Eloquence describes the quality of speech or writing itself, not the person -- we say someone 'speaks with eloquence' or 'writes with eloquence,' and the related adjective is 'eloquent.'
